prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Context: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) NextGen improves National Airspace System (NAS) capacity/efficiency. National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Airspace Technology Demonstrations 3 (ATD-3) integrates ground/aircraft aids for weather avoidance, Traffic Management Initiatives (TMIs), and en-route/arrival metering.
Actors/elements: FAA traffic managers; air traffic control/controllers; aircraft; aircraft/flight operators; airline flight dispatchers; pilots/flight crews; public; industry; air traffic management (ATM) stakeholders; flight management systems; onboard weather radar.
Operations: TMIs divert/meter aircraft; managers designate forecast-convection Flow Constrained Areas (FCAs). Severe Weather Avoidance Plans (SWAP), alias Playbook routes, address constraints 2–8 hours ahead. Dispatchers must file plans ≥45 minutes before push-back and select/revise SWAP routes. Collaborative Trajectory Options Program (CTOP) receives operator route options/departure-delay preferences; no postdeparture optimization. Crews coordinate alternatives with controllers/dispatchers; conflict avoidance requires controller coordination.
Dynamic Weather Routes (DWR), NASA ground automation extending Direct-To, continuously analyzes flights ≥10,000 ft using radar tracks, flight plans, weather/airspace/traffic data for wind-corrected time/fuel-saving amendments. Maneuver Start Point (MSP) defaults five minutes downstream or first high-altitude-airspace point. Return Capture Fix (RCF) rejoins current Center flight plan; Center-specific limit function considers aircraft position, routing, arrival limits and possibly adjacent Centers; generally not last in-Center fix. Fort Worth Center (ZFW) implementation uses rectangle extending ~200 nmi beyond boundary.
MSP–RCF direct reference must meet configurable savings (default five minutes); weather/traffic probing follows. Weather resolution inserts one/two minimum-delay fix-radial-distance auxiliary waypoints; optional snap-to replaces these with nearby named fixes. Qualifying weather-clear, optionally traffic-clear, solutions enter display alert list. Both trajectories undergo congestion/Special Use Airspace (SUA) analysis; status displayed. Selecting advisory activates trial planning; users modify MSP/RCF/waypoints; savings/conflict status updates automatically within one second. Interface strongly warns of conflicts; users request/issue clearance. Polygon avoidance supports nonweather obstacles. No formal modes; FAA implementation unspecified.

New part:
U0077: The default RCF is either the last flight plan fix inside the limit rectangle or, for aircraft landing inside the limit rectangle, the last fix before the arrival STAR.
U0078: Another approach is to analyze historically observed direct route clearances in each Center and use frequently occurring direct route clearances to define a convex limit polygon.
U0079: In this approach the limit polygon replaces the simpler limit rectangle, but the fix selection logic is otherwise the same.
U0080: This empirically derived limit polygon approach has been implemented in the Future ATM Concept Evaluation Tool (FACET) implementation of DWR called National Airspace System Constraint Evaluation and Notification Tool (NASCENT).
U0081: Other methods, such as choosing the RCF based on the particular city pair routing within a Center, could also be implemented.
U0082: Figure 3: Capture Fix Limit Regions (rectangle and polygon) Early in the testing of DWR at American Airlines, users identified the need for an MSP in the DWR trajectory modeling.
U0083: Depending on workload and other factors, users may need several minutes of coordination time before the point at which a flight is expected to depart the current trajectory to fly a DWR route.
U0084: An MSP located a user-definable number of minutes downstream of present position on the current flight plan trajectory, or for climbing flights, the point at which the flight is predicted to be in high-altitude airspace (FL240 for ZFW), enables users to see the effect of coordination delay on trajectory status parameters like weather proximity, flying time savings, traffic conflicts, and level flight status, which is particularly important for climbing flights that may not have reached the high altitude airspace.
U0085: Five minutes was generally the accepted default value used during the trials with American Airlines [3].
U0086: All DWR advisories initially incorporate the default MSP.
U0087: Once in trial planning, the user may adjust the MSP using click and drag inputs and assess the effect on status parameters.
U0088: If the MSP is within 10 nmi of a flight plan fix, the MSP snaps to the flight plan fix.
U0089: Auxiliary waypoints are added when needed to avoid weather, or optionally weather and traffic, and provide the minimum-delay route based on geometry and winds.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
